open.say: Every document pipeline starts with one question: which way is up?

fail.say: Pipelines guess the quarter turn first, then remove the tilt. But classifiers only ever saw level pages: on this tilted page, the guess is half a turn off, and the deskewer levels it, perfectly upside down.

insight.say: Here's the fix. Any angle is a quarter turn, plus a tilt under forty-five degrees. Rows of text reveal the tilt. Letter shapes reveal the turn.

level.say: So LevelHead deskews first. Text rows draw a streak in the Fourier spectrum; we read its angle, and turn the page level.

hann.say: On phone photos, the borders outshine the text. A Hann taper fades them, and the streak returns.

ask.say: Then any frozen model looks at the level page four times, once per quarter turn.

roll.say: Each answer is rolled back by its turn, and the four are multiplied. A model's favourite answer cancels out, and one confidently wrong view is simply outvoted.

any.say: No training. It wraps any model, from a mobile CNN to a two-hundred-billion-parameter VLM.

results.say: Classify-first collapses at every diagonal. LevelHead stays flat, and on tilted pages every model gains, by up to sixty points.

real.say: On real phone photos and scans, classifiers climb from two thirds to ninety percent.

scores.say: Two tests, two scores. Guessing the angle: vision-language models gain thirty-eight points on average, classifiers seven. Reading the text: OCR errors fall to the level of a perfectly upright page.
